title: If the Lord wills (James 4:11–17)
hook: you are a mist that appears for a little while

segments.voice: Yesterday, draw near to God, and your line was draw near. When a fight rose inside you, did you take a step back toward stillness first? Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Open your calendar app. Look at next month. There it is, all laid out in neat colored blocks: the trip, the deadline, the dentist, the dinner. It looks so certain on the screen. Now think back to a year ago. How much of what you planned then actually happened the way you planned it? James is writing to people who did business across the Roman world, merchants who traveled from city to city to trade. And he speaks to them in a voice that sounds like he's reading over their shoulder as they plan.

First a quick word against speaking evil of one another: there is one judge, he says, so who are you to judge your neighbor? Then the business plan. In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain." Today or tomorrow. Such a city. A year. Profit. It's very specific, and very confident. Then James says: "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." A vapor. The breath you see on a cold morning. The steam off a cup of coffee. The mist on a field at dawn that's gone by nine. It's there, it's real, and then it isn't. James doesn't say, so don't plan. He gives them better words for planning: "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that." Make the plan. Hold it with an open hand. Christians took this into everyday speech for centuries. Some still write the Latin letters D.V., Deo volente, God willing, at the bottom of a letter about future plans. Muslims say something close, in sha' Allah, if God wills, and many Jews say im yirtzeh Hashem. It's a shared human humility about tomorrow. And the passage ends with a line that turns the whole thing around: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin." If life is a vapor, the good you know you could do is for today. Not someday.

Here's the practice: plan loosely today. Settle, and breathe. Picture your plans for the rest of today and tomorrow, block by block. Now imagine each one written on a little card, and you holding the cards in an open hand instead of a fist. Feel the difference in your hand. Notice which plan you're gripping hardest. Breathe out slowly, and watch your breath disappear, the way James's vapor does. Then think of one good thing you know you could do today and have been putting off. If you pray, you can offer your plans to God. The bell holds the time.
If the Lord wills. James's words for every plan: we shall live and do this or that, held with an open hand, because life is a vapor.
Your line: a little while. Today, do the one good thing you've been saving for someday, while it's still today. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians add "God willing" or "Lord willing" when speaking of future plans, and some still write D.V., for Deo volente, at the end of a letter or a notice of meetings.

original.note: Greek: vapor, mist, steam. the root of the English word atmosphere.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy reminder that life is short.
what it means: plan, but hold plans open-handed, and don't put off the good you can do today.
what a scholar hears: atmis, vapor, the root of atmosphere, and a habit of speech, Deo volente, that Christians carried for centuries.
